subtopic_detail: Scant periods with cyclical pain six months after surgical evacuation for retained products of conception
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who gave birth fourteen months ago. She had a 1500 mL postpartum haemorrhage and underwent suction evacuation of retained products at day nine, which was repeated a fortnight later for continued bleeding.

Her periods returned six months ago as a single day of brown staining and have since become one or two hours of light spotting each cycle. Every month, two days before the spotting, she gets deep central pelvic cramping that lasts about 36 hours and settles when the spotting starts. She stopped breastfeeding four months ago, has not resumed contraception and would like another pregnancy. Her pregnancy test is negative. Her follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, oestradiol, prolactin and thyroid stimulating hormone are all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, normal vulva and vagina, cervix appears normal, uterus anteverted, normal size, non tender
data_table.Investigations: Beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (3-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 5.1 IU/L (2-10 follicular), oestradiol 320 pmol/L (100-400 follicular), prolactin 240 mIU/L (100-500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that lactational suppression explains the pattern and review her again in six months
options.rationale: She stopped breastfeeding four months ago and her gonadotropins and oestradiol show normal ovarian cycling, so suppression of the axis is excluded. Further waiting delays treatment while adhesions mature and become harder to divide (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill for three months to establish a regular bleeding pattern
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy cannot restore an endometrium that has been replaced by fibrous adhesions, and it also blocks the pregnancy she is seeking. Cyclical hormones treat anovulatory bleeding disturbance, which her normal hormone profile argues against (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

options.text: Perform a progestogen withdrawal test and diagnose premature ovarian insufficiency if she does not bleed
options.rationale: A withdrawal test cannot distinguish an unresponsive endometrium from an outflow obstruction, and her normal follicle stimulating hormone with a normal oestradiol already excludes ovarian insufficiency. The near pair to keep separate here is a hormonal cause versus a structural one (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

options.text: Refer her for hysteroscopy so the cavity can be inspected and any adhesions divided at the same time
options.rationale: Repeated instrumentation of a puerperal uterus is the classic cause of intrauterine adhesions, and normal ovarian hormones with cyclical pain preceding scant flow indicate a normally cycling endometrium meeting an obstructed cavity. Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the treatment, allowing adhesiolysis under direct vision (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).
source_refs: Human Reproduction Update: Intrauterine adhesions after pregnancy related curettage

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to characterise the uterus before any intervention
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is used to define congenital uterine anomalies rather than to detect intrauterine adhesions, which it images poorly. Saline infusion sonohysterography is the non invasive alternative when hysteroscopy must be deferred (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea or markedly reduced flow after uterine instrumentation, particularly curettage of a recently pregnant uterus, should raise intrauterine adhesions before any endocrine cause is entertained. The puerperal endometrium is thin and vulnerable, so evacuation after postpartum haemorrhage or for retained products carries the highest risk, and a repeat procedure multiplies it. The diagnostic logic is that normal gonadotropins and oestradiol with cyclical symptoms indicate ovulation is occurring, placing the lesion in the outflow tract. Cyclical pain reflects trapped menstrual blood behind partial obstruction. Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis restores menses in most women and improves subsequent fertility, though adhesions recur in a significant minority and postoperative strategies to keep the cavity apart are used.
key_points: Instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus is the dominant risk factor for intrauterine adhesions
Normal gonadotropins and oestradiol place the problem in the outflow tract, not the ovary
Cyclical pain preceding scant flow suggests obstructed menstrual outflow
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the definitive treatment
Magnetic resonance imaging is for congenital anomalies and images adhesions poorly
explanation.pearls: Delaying any repeat evacuation until at least a few weeks postpartum, and using ultrasound guidance when it is unavoidable, is the main preventive measure, since adhesion risk is highest when the endometrium is curetted between two and four weeks after birth.

sources.label: Human Reproduction Update: Intrauterine adhesions after pregnancy related curettage

subtopic_detail: Markedly increased nuchal translucency at twelve weeks with a structurally normal appearing fetus
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 38 year old woman who is 12 weeks and four days into her first pregnancy. She had a combined first trimester screening test three days ago.

The nuchal translucency measured 4.6 mm with a crown rump length of 63 mm, and the fetus appeared structurally normal with a visible nasal bone and normal ductus venosus flow. Her biochemistry gave a combined risk of 1 in 15 for trisomy 21. She and her partner say they want as much information as possible as early as possible, and would consider termination for a serious abnormality. She has no family history of genetic disease and her booking bloods, including her blood group, were unremarkable. She is well and the pregnancy is a spontaneous conception.

data_table.Imaging: Nuchal translucency 4.6 mm at a crown rump length of 63 mm, nasal bone present, normal ductus venosus a wave, no structural abnormality visible, single live fetus
data_table.Investigations: Combined first trimester screening risk 1 in 15 for trisomy 21, blood group A positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about further testing?

options.text: Arrange non invasive prenatal testing of cell free DNA and proceed further only if it is high risk
options.rationale: Cell free DNA screening interrogates a small number of chromosomes and would miss the copy number variants, rare aneuploidies and single gene disorders that a translucency of this size is associated with. It is the better choice when the translucency is normal and the risk comes from age or biochemistry alone (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Repeat the nuchal translucency measurement in two weeks and decide on testing from that result
options.rationale: The measurement is only valid between a crown rump length of 45 and 84 mm, so it cannot meaningfully be repeated later, and translucency often resolves while the underlying abnormality remains. Waiting also removes the option of a first trimester diagnostic procedure (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Defer all further testing until the detailed morphology scan at twenty weeks demonstrates the anatomy
options.rationale: A normal morphology scan reduces but does not exclude a genetic diagnosis, and deferring removes the earlier and safer testing window the couple have said they want. Anatomy assessment complements genetic testing rather than replacing it (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Book amniocentesis at fifteen weeks as the safest way to obtain a definitive genetic result for her
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is a legitimate diagnostic route with a comparable loss rate in experienced hands, but it delays a definitive answer by nearly three weeks in a couple who have asked for the earliest possible information. It becomes the preferred option when the presentation is later or when placental mosaicism would confuse the result (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Offer chorionic villus sampling now with chromosomal microarray testing of the sample obtained
options.rationale: A translucency of 3.5 mm or more carries a wide range of causes beyond the common trisomies, including copy number variants and structural cardiac disease, so a diagnostic sample analysed by microarray is the test that answers the question. Sampling in the first trimester delivers the result in the window the couple have identified as important to them (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities
Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Prenatal diagnosis policy

explanation.summary: Nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more is a marker of a broad group of conditions rather than of trisomy 21 alone, and roughly a third of affected fetuses have a chromosomal abnormality while many of the remainder have structural heart disease, skeletal dysplasia, a genetic syndrome or a copy number variant. This is the reason a diagnostic test with chromosomal microarray outperforms screening based on cell free DNA in this setting, since screening reports only on the chromosomes it targets. Chorionic villus sampling is available from 11 weeks and amniocentesis from 15 weeks, and both carry a procedure related loss rate of well under one per cent in experienced units. Even after normal genetic results, a fetus with increased translucency needs a detailed cardiac assessment because the association with congenital heart disease persists. Counselling should set out what each test can and cannot exclude before a choice is made.
key_points: Increased nuchal translucency is a marker for a broad range of genetic and structural conditions
Cell free DNA screening reports only on targeted chromosomes and misses copy number variants
Chromosomal microarray on a diagnostic sample is the higher yield test in this situation
Chorionic villus sampling from 11 weeks gives an earlier answer than amniocentesis from 15 weeks
Fetal echocardiography is indicated even when genetic testing returns normal
explanation.pearls: A nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more justifies a fetal echocardiogram at around 20 weeks regardless of the genetic result, because congenital heart disease is found in roughly 3 to 5 per cent of these pregnancies with normal chromosomes.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities
Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Prenatal diagnosis policy

subtopic_detail: Deep unconsciousness at a dance party with bradycardia and no response to an opioid antagonist
stem:
You are the emergency registrar receiving a 22 year old man brought in by ambulance from a warehouse party. His friends say he drank two beers and swallowed a capful of a clear liquid from a water bottle about forty minutes ago.

He is deeply unconscious and snoring, with no response to voice and localisation to a trapezius squeeze. His pupils are 4 mm and reactive, his blood sugar is 6.4 mmol/L, and he has no head injury or neck tenderness. Paramedics gave 800 micrograms of intranasal naloxone with no change in his conscious state. With a jaw thrust and a lateral position his airway is clear, he ventilates spontaneously with good chest movement, and his saturations sit at 98 per cent on 6 L per minute by mask. His temperature is normal and there is no rigidity or clonus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 48 per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on 6 L per minute by mask, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 7, pupils 4 mm and reactive, no clonus or rigidity, airway patent with jaw thrust in the lateral position
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous blood gas pH 7.34 with pCO2 48 mmHg, electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue airway positioning with close monitoring in a resuscitation bay and observe for spontaneous waking
options.rationale: Gamma hydroxybutyrate produces abrupt deep coma with bradycardia and a patent airway that reverses spontaneously over one to four hours, so meticulous airway support and monitoring avoid an unnecessary intubation. The failure to respond to naloxone with normal pupils is the finding that separates this from opioid poisoning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give a further larger dose of intravenous naloxone titrated upwards until he regains consciousness
options.rationale: Escalating an opioid antagonist is futile when an adequate initial dose has produced no response and the pupils are mid sized rather than pinpoint. Higher doses are justified when partial response suggests a long acting or high potency opioid (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil to reverse a presumed benzodiazepine effect and reassess him
options.rationale: Flumazenil risks precipitating seizures in a patient with unknown co ingestants and possible benzodiazepine dependence, and it has no effect on this class of drug. Its narrow role is in iatrogenic oversedation with a known single agent (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and give activated charcoal to reduce further absorption of the ingested liquid
options.rationale: Charcoal binds this compound poorly, the ingestion was over half an hour ago, and instilling it into an unprotected airway risks aspiration pneumonitis. Decontamination is considered for early large ingestions of adsorbable toxins in a protected airway (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Perform rapid sequence intubation now on the grounds that his coma score is below the usual threshold
options.rationale: A coma score alone does not mandate intubation when the airway is patent, gas exchange is adequate and rapid spontaneous recovery is expected within hours. Intubation is indicated if he vomits, desaturates, loses his gag or fails to improve as predicted (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Gamma hydroxybutyrate and its precursors are used recreationally for euphoria and have an extremely narrow margin between the recreational and the anaesthetic dose, which is why coma after a small volume of an unlabelled liquid is a common Australian emergency presentation. The characteristic picture is sudden profound coma with bradycardia, preserved respiratory drive, normal pupils and no response to naloxone, followed by abrupt agitated awakening. Because the drug is cleared rapidly, most patients recover within one to four hours and can be managed with airway positioning and monitoring, avoiding the complications of intubation. Deterioration, vomiting, or failure to wake within the expected window should prompt reassessment for co ingestion or another cause such as head injury. Regular users can develop dependence with a severe withdrawal syndrome resembling delirium tremens, which requires high dose benzodiazepines.
key_points: Profound coma with bradycardia, normal pupils and preserved ventilation suggests this class of drug
Absent response to an adequate naloxone dose argues against opioid poisoning
Recovery is typically abrupt within one to four hours
A low coma score alone does not mandate intubation when the airway is patent and gas exchange is adequate
Flumazenil is hazardous with unknown co ingestants and does not reverse this agent
explanation.pearls: Withdrawal in a dependent user begins within hours of the last dose and can require very large cumulative diazepam doses, so ask specifically about daily dosing intervals in anyone presenting with agitation and tremor after this drug.

subtopic_detail: Seizure at a music festival after a stimulant and large volumes of water with a serum sodium of 118
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to a 19 year old woman who had a two minute generalised seizure in the department. Her friends say she took two tablets sold as ecstasy about six hours ago and has been drinking water steadily all evening because she was worried about overheating.

She vomited twice before the seizure and had complained of a severe headache. She is now drowsy but rousable and has not seized again. Her temperature is normal, her skin is dry, and there is no rigidity, clonus or trismus. She takes no regular medication and has no history of epilepsy. Her serum sodium is 118 mmol/L, her serum osmolality is 248 mOsm/kg, her urine osmolality is 620 mOsm/kg and her urine sodium is 58 mmol/L. Her creatine kinase is 210 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 58 mmol/L, creatine kinase 210 U/L (less than 200), capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Restrict her fluid intake to 800 mL daily and recheck her serum sodium in six hours time
options.rationale: Fluid restriction alone corrects sodium far too slowly for a patient who has already seized, leaving her at risk of further seizures and cerebral herniation. Restriction is the treatment for asymptomatic or chronic hyponatraemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give a bolus of hypertonic 3 per cent saline and reassess her symptoms and sodium afterwards
options.rationale: Severe hyponatraemia with seizures is a neurological emergency requiring a rapid small rise in serum sodium, achieved with a bolus of hypertonic saline that can be repeated until symptoms resolve. The aim is a rise of about 4 to 6 mmol/L to relieve cerebral oedema rather than full correction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Infuse two litres of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride over four hours and monitor her urine output
options.rationale: Isotonic saline given to a patient with high urine osmolality from antidiuretic hormone excess can paradoxically lower the sodium further as the salt is excreted and the water retained. It is appropriate when hyponatraemia is driven by hypovolaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol to reduce cerebral oedema and arrange urgent computed tomography
options.rationale: An osmotic diuretic loses free water and solute in an unpredictable ratio and is not the agent of choice for hyponatraemic encephalopathy. Imaging is warranted if she fails to improve or has focal signs, but it must not delay correction of the sodium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Commence dantrolene and active cooling for presumed serotonergic hyperthermia from the tablets
options.rationale: She is normothermic with a near normal creatine kinase and no rigidity or clonus, so the hyperthermic toxidrome is not present. That syndrome is the other classic life threat with this drug and is treated with cooling, benzodiazepines and sometimes dantrolene (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Two mechanisms combine to produce dangerous hyponatraemia after methylenedioxymethamphetamine use, namely drug induced release of antidiuretic hormone and the deliberate drinking of large volumes of water to prevent overheating. Young women appear disproportionately affected. Because the fall in sodium happens over hours, the brain has no time to adapt and cerebral oedema develops at levels that would be tolerated in chronic hyponatraemia. The urine osmolality above serum osmolality with a raised urine sodium confirms inappropriate antidiuresis rather than simple water intoxication with suppressed hormone. Correction targets symptom resolution with a rise of a few millimoles per litre, and the total rise is capped over 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination, although that complication is rare in acute presentations.
key_points: The mechanism is antidiuretic hormone release plus excessive free water intake
Seizure with severe hyponatraemia is treated with hypertonic saline, not fluid restriction
Aim for a rise of about 4 to 6 mmol/L acutely and cap the 24 hour rise
Isotonic saline may worsen the sodium when antidiuretic hormone activity is high
Normothermia with a normal creatine kinase argues against the hyperthermic toxidrome
explanation.pearls: Limit correction to about 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours even after an acute drop, and consider desmopressin with free water if an unexpected water diuresis threatens to overshoot that ceiling.

subtopic_detail: Third relapse of psychotic depression within months of two successful acute electroconvulsive therapy courses
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68 year old woman in the outpatient clinic. Over eighteen months she has had two episodes of severe depression with nihilistic delusions, each of which responded fully to a course of electroconvulsive therapy after failing to improve on medication.

After the second course she was maintained on venlafaxine at a therapeutic dose with lithium augmentation, and a dispensing record confirms she has collected every prescription. Her lithium level a fortnight ago was 0.72 mmol/L and her thyroid function and renal function are normal. Over the past three weeks she has again stopped eating, is sleeping two hours a night and has begun saying her bowels have rotted away. She scores 26 on a depression rating scale. Her cognition between episodes has returned to her baseline and she lives independently with her husband.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, poor oral intake, nihilistic delusions concerning her abdomen, no thoughts of self harm elicited but limited engagement
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 maintenance), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2, full blood examination and electrolytes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long term treatment plan once this episode is treated?

options.text: Switch her antidepressant to a tricyclic agent and continue outpatient review every four weeks
options.rationale: She has relapsed repeatedly despite an adequately dosed antidepressant with lithium augmentation, so a further medication switch has a low probability of preventing the next episode. A switch is the logical step when relapse follows an inadequate trial or poor adherence (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Increase the lithium dose to achieve a level at the upper end of the therapeutic range for her
options.rationale: Her level already sits within the maintenance range and pushing it higher in a 68 year old raises the risk of neurotoxicity and renal injury without evidence of preventing further relapse. Dose increase is reasonable when the level is subtherapeutic (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange maintenance electroconvulsive therapy at spaced intervals alongside her current medication
options.rationale: Repeated relapse soon after a successful acute course, in a patient whose illness reliably responds to that treatment and not to medication, is the recognised indication for continuation and maintenance electroconvulsive therapy delivered at progressively spaced intervals. It reduces relapse rates compared with medication alone in this group (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on electroconvulsive therapy).
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on electroconvulsive therapy
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy delivered weekly as the mainstay of relapse prevention
options.rationale: Structured psychotherapy has a limited role as sole prevention in severe psychotic depression, where the acuity and delusional content impair engagement. It has value as an adjunct once the episode has remitted (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Add a second generation antipsychotic and reduce the frequency of her clinic reviews accordingly
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is standard within an episode of psychotic depression but has not held her well between episodes, and reducing review frequency in a patient with a relapsing severe illness is unsafe. Adding it without addressing the relapse pattern repeats what has already failed (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy has the highest response rate of any treatment for severe depression with psychotic features, but relapse after an acute course is common and is the main limitation of the treatment. Continuation therapy in the six months after remission and maintenance therapy beyond that are used when relapse has occurred despite adequate pharmacotherapy, when previous courses have been rapidly effective, and when the patient prefers it. Sessions are typically spaced from weekly to fortnightly and then monthly, with the interval guided by symptom re emergence. Cognitive effects are monitored formally because anterograde memory disturbance is the principal adverse effect, and the older patient with independent baseline function tolerates spaced treatments well. Consent requirements and review by a second practitioner are set out in each state and territory mental health act.
key_points: Relapse after a successful acute course despite adequate medication is the indication for continuation therapy
Intervals are spaced progressively and titrated against symptom re emergence
Response to previous courses strongly predicts response to maintenance therapy
Formal cognitive monitoring is part of every maintenance program
Antidepressant and lithium therapy usually continue alongside rather than being stopped
explanation.pearls: Lithium is continued during maintenance electroconvulsive therapy in most protocols but is often withheld on the morning of treatment, since higher levels around the time of the seizure are associated with prolonged confusion.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on electroconvulsive therapy
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
